Chapter 10. Remembering What Was Lost, Imagining What Can Be Restored.
You know that quiet ache you get when you realize something precious is gone? Maybe it’s an old photograph, a faded map, or just a story someone in your family used to tell. All these little fragments, they hint at a world that used to be—wilder, richer, teeming with life in ways we can barely imagine now.
Sometimes, it’s easy to think the damage is done. That the wild things are gone for good, and there’s no way back. But here’s the thing—the story isn’t over yet.
Picture this: there’s a remote valley, and a group of volunteers is gathered along a stream, quietly planting trees. Their hands dig into the soil, but their minds are somewhere in the future, picturing the forest that could one day rise up here.
Then a child—a little too young to remember the wolves that once roamed these hills—asks a simple question: “Will they ever come back?” The adults pause, not quite sure how to answer. But the question hangs in the air, like a tiny seed of hope, planted right alongside those young trees.
Somewhere else, an elder is sharing stories about when the rivers ran thick with salmon and the hills echoed with the cries of eagles. The young people listening? Their eyes go wide, and just for a moment, it’s like the past is close enough to touch.
Those stories—they aren’t just memories. They’re blueprints for what could be possible again.
See, restoration isn’t about trying to turn back the clock. It’s about learning from what came before, honoring what was lost, and using our imaginations to picture what might still be.
It’s about making space for wildness—not just out there in the landscape, but right here, in our hearts and minds.
Most of us will never see the world exactly as it once was. But every single one of us can help shape what it will become. The work is slow, sure. There are setbacks. But the rewards? They’re real. A world that’s richer, more resilient, more alive.
The wild things might be gone from many places, but their story’s not finished—not yet. With a little care, some courage, and a whole lot of imagination, it’s possible to bring them back. Not just as echoes of the past, but as partners in the world we’re building together.
